newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan forsakes Islamic weekend on PM's order.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan forsakes Islamic weekend on PM's order.

text.p: Pakistan formally gave up the Islamic weekend on Friday, after more 20 years of observing it, in a bold switchover ordered by new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif.
The change was marked by mild protests from fundamentalist Islamic circles, particularly the right-wing Jamaat-i-Islami party.

Sharif personally ordered the switchover to a one-day Sunday weekend from Friday in a televised address on Sunday, six days after taking office following his Pakistan Muslim League's landslide victory in February 3 elections.

All government offices opened on Friday, although only for half a day to allow time for traditional Moslem prayers. Most businesses, including banks, and the country's three stock exchanges also heeded Sharif's call.
But some businessmen kept their shops closed while the Jamaat-i-Islami party held small protests in several cities.
Friday was declared an Islamic weekend in Pakistan in the 1970s by then-Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto to appease Islamic clergy.
Traders were unhappy with the move because of its effect on their trade with non-Islamic countries which treat Fridays as normal working days.
Subsequent moves to revert back to a Sunday weekend failed because of fears of a backlash from fundamentalist Islamic clergy.

Sharif, whose landslide election win has given him the flexibility to take tough action, decided on the change even before forming a cabinet, arguing that the Friday holiday had been used more for social occasions than for prayers.
"To give Friday its due status and to restore its sanctity, we have decided to have the holiday on Sunday," he said in his speech on Sunday.
But he said offices would close at midday so that people could go to mosques for traditional Islamic congregations.
